extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate public interested in morals, manners, and literary criticism (early 18th-century urban readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Short didactic and critical essays (Spectator-style) offering rules and observations about love, criticism, rhetoric, dreams, and social conduct for a general literate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love casuistry — judging fine points of courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: Give judgments on nice and intricate cases which can happen in an Amour (examples supplied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondent offers concrete micro-rules/questions for resolving amorous situations, e.g., How great the Contraction of the Fingers must be before it amounts to a Squeeze by the Hand; What can be properly termed an absolute Denial from a Maid, and what from a Widow; What Advances a Lover may presume to make, after having received a Patt upon his Shoulder from his Mistress's Fan; Whether a Lady, at the first Interview, may allow an Humble Servant to kiss her Hand; How far it may be permitted to caress the Maid in order to succeed with the Mistress; What Constructions a Man may put upon a Smile, and in what Cases a Frown goes for nothing; On what Occasions a sheepish Look may do Service, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims on the nature and effects of Love
rubrics_metrics.description: Pithy aphorisms about love summarizing its social/psychological effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a set of compact rules/observations such as: 'There are more Calamities in the World arising from Love than from Hatred.'; 'Love is the Daughter of Idleness, but the Mother of Disquietude.'; 'A Coquet often loses her Reputation, whilst she preserves her Virtue.'; 'A Prude often preserves her Reputation when she has lost her Virtue.'; 'Love refines a Man's Behaviour, but makes a Woman's ridiculous.'; 'Love is generally accompanied with Good-will in the Young, Interest in the Middle-aged, and a Passion too gross to Name in the Old.'; and other similar maxims used as practical heuristics about conduct and appearance in matters of love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss a popular play solely because it runs long
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics who claim 'That whatever Dramatick Performance has a long Run, must of Necessity be good for nothing' are mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues against the rule among some critics that a long-running play must be bad; observes this maxim is used to attack successful pieces rather than judge them by intrinsic qualities. Implicitly recommends judges evaluate plays on their merits (and the primary purpose of poetry/drama: to please) rather than on length of run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim of poetry/drama: to please
rubrics_metrics.description: The first precept in Poetry is not to please (i.e., poetry should aim to please).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopts the position that pleasing the audience is a principal objective of poetry and drama; thus criticism should not subordinate pleasure to rigid adherence to rules. This defends works that 'take' (please) the public even if they deviate from formal precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and virtues of a true critic
rubrics_metrics.description: A true critic should be learned, have taste, and be able to discover beauties and excuse little slips as the ancient critics do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given to classical exemplars (Aristotle, Longinus, Horace, Quintilian, Boileau, Dacier). True critics 'discover Beauties which escaped the Observation of the Vulgar' and 'very often find out Reasons for palliating and excusing such little Slips and Oversights.' The essay criticizes modern smatterers who lack learning (do not know how to put ten Words together with Elegance), criticise only at second-hand, misuse technical words (unity, action, sentiment, diction) as jargon, and thus should cultivate learning, taste, and humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid envy, cavil, and detraction in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Envy and cavil are the natural fruits of laziness and ignorance, and lead to depreciating every successful production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links malicious criticism to moral failings: idle or ignorant men are apt to detract from others, producing 'imaginary Blemishes' and far-fetched arguments to make celebrated beauties appear as faults. Critics should be mindful of these motives and avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow deviations from the rules where they produce the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: There is sometimes greater judgment in deviating from the Rules of Art than in adhering to them; the Sublime or 'Gusto Grande' may require breaking rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay asserts many great writers and artists knowingly depart from established rules when such departures produce nobler effects; examples from tragic writers and from architecture/statuary are cited. It further states that works of a great genius who is ignorant of rules often have more beauty than works of a little genius who scrupulously observes them (Terence's sentiment quoted). Shakespeare is offered as the supreme example: born with 'all the Seeds of Poetry' and often violating formal stage rules with superior results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the mixture of inconsistent metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mixture of inconsistent Metaphors is a fault producing confusion, obscurity, and noise; metaphors must be homogeneous and sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines metaphor as an image affecting the senses and warns against combining images from different senses or making metaphorical beings perform actions impossible for their originals ('The heavy Lashes that have dropped from your Pen' is ridiculed). Gives rule-of-thumb: metaphors/images based on sight should not be applied to hearing, etc. Also warns against metaphors running into tedious allegories (wandering from the subject for a page) and provides an example letter filled with mixed metaphors as an anti-pattern. Suggests readers can judge metaphor consistency by picturing the image literally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination rules to avoid spreading scandal and calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: Three checks to examine one's heart before accusing oneself of not being guilty of spreading calumny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three rules: (1) Consider whether you take delight in hearing the faults of others; (2) Whether you are too apt to believe little blackening accounts and more inclined to be credulous on the uncharitable side; (3) Whether you are ready to spread and propagate reports tending to another's disreputation. These mark the progressive steps by which vice grows into slander and defamation; remedy is to extinguish the temptation and keep secrets within one's own breast.

rubrics_metrics.name: When hearing accusations: practise charity and restraint (Abbey de la Trappe rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for members of the Abbey de la Trappe about handling reports of base or criminal actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advised conduct: never give an ear to accounts of base or criminal actions; turn off such discourse if possible; but if one hears something so well attested that disbelief is impossible, then suppose the criminal action may have proceeded from a good intention in the guilty person. This counsel favors charity and suppression of scandal over credulous propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat dreams as material for moral and practical reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine imaginary scenes in sleep because they may contain traces leading to noble thoughts; render sleep improving by managing waking life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dreams are likened to a map for a traveller: even if not literally real, their traces can lead to proper paths of action. Dreams often conform to waking thoughts and arise from day's occurrences, temper at lying down, or perhaps direction from a superior being. Practical guidance: make a 'good Day' if you wish a 'good Night'; fix thoughts while awake to influence dream content; use dreams as indications of the 'divine part' within us. The correspondent also suggests noting dreams to learn from them (e.g., arranging activities to produce beneficial dreams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use noisy morning criers as reminders to return to reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than suppressing those who rouse the city early, regard them as remembrancers to admonish wakeful dreamers to return to their true condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay offers the pragmatic, almost satirical suggestion that morning criers who disturb dreamers can be seen as kindly reminders (like the Macedonian prince's attendant who reminded him he was a man) to stop fantasizing and prepare to act suitably to one's real circumstances. Thus, transform nuisance into a useful social function.
